newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dollar sandwiched in a very stale range.
newsitem.headline: Australian dollar sandwiched in a very stale range.

text.p: The Australian dollar was the rather limp filling in a very stale range Monday, sandwiched between exporter and options-related bids and offers from mostly U.S. investment banks and Japanese securities houses.
This was the start of its sixth week in a US$0.7720/7860 band and dealers had become ever more cautious in their trading strategies, prefering to play tight ranges for a quick turn.

Some harboured hopes the deadlock would end soon since the Federal Reserve was meeting Tuesday to decide whether to hike U.S. interest rates and key domestic wages data out Wednesday and Thursday could open or close the door for an easing here.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local currency was lying at US$0.7745/50 having barely shifted from an early US$0.7749/54 and Friday's late US$0.7750/55.
There was a brief burst of action on the crosses when the yen surged in response to a huge jump in Japan's trade surplus, but quickly retraced in the face of surprisingly heavy selling.
The local dollar bounced to 89.93/03 yen in late trade from a 89.07 trough, but was still short of Friday's 90.50/60.
Japan's April trade surplus ballooned by 164 percent on the same month last year to reach 831 billion yen, while the surplus with the U.S. rose an even stronger 174 percent.

The rise in the surplus was largely due to the lengthy weakness of the yen and was expected to stretch for a few months yet. That in turn was likely to strain Japan's trade relations with the U.S. as well as pointing to a sharp increase in the net demand for yen by offshore buyers of Japanese goods.
The U.S. dollar took it hard at first, falling over 1/2 yen to 115.00 in minutes, but by the close had rallied to 116.03/13.

Trader were reluctant to go aggressively short of the dollar given the not inconsiderable chance the Fed would hike U.S. rates tomorrow. Market opinion was split down the middle and many felt that, in this case, it was trendy to be square.
If the Fed did raise its funds rate to 5.75 percent it would narrow the gap with official Australian rates, and thus the A$'s short term yield advantage, to just 25 basis points.
Dealers expected to see US$0.7720 again on such an outcome with a breach producing a fall to US$0.7680 or even US$0.7635.

The market was also haunted by the risk of another rate cut here, even though no lesser authority than Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane had recently said he was concerned by firm wages growth and saw no economic benefit in a further easing.
But analysts could not help but note that aggragate wages growth had been inflated by the public sector for most of 1996.
This was thought to be a function of wide-scale redundancies among lower paid public workers which helped boost average weekly wage growth to an annual 7.6 percent in Q4 last year.

In contrast private sector earnings -- which are far more relevant to inflationary pressures in the economy -- had been running at just 2.8 percent year-on-year in Q4, so another subdued result this time could leave space for a cut.

Analysts said annual growth was likely to rise this time since a low 0.3 percent quarterly rise from Q1 1996 would fall out of the calculation, and anything above 3.5 percent yr-on-yr would certainly alarm the RBA.

A survey of wage trends from HSBC Markets today did not bode well on this front. It found wages growth in enterprise bargaining agreements probably picked up in the March quarter to around 4.65 percent from the 4.4 percent reported by the Department of Industrial Relations (DIR) in Q4.

HSBC Markets economist Grant Fitzner said growth had been driven by a jump in private sector wage bargains and he expected the DIR measure of private sector wages would rise to around 4.9 percent from an annual 4.4 percent in Q4 1996.
The DIR is aiming to release its wage data at 11.30 am (0130 GMT) on Wednesday. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
